working_title: The Dead Man Who Fooled Hitler: Operation Mincemeat
hook: An entire army's survival hung on a single, impossible question: could a dead man convince Adolf Hitler to walk straight into a trap?
structure: Countdown of the key moments that led to the outcome, building tension toward the final one.

chapters.title: The Trout Memo and the Trap

scenes.narration: An entire army's survival hung on a single, impossible question: could a dead man convince Adolf Hitler to walk straight into a trap? In late 1942, Allied forces in North Africa stood victorious, but a massive strategic dilemma loomed over what to do next. Prime Minister Winston Churchill wanted to strike at Europe's soft underbelly, but the path ahead was painfully obvious to everyone watching.

shots.title: The Trout Memo and the Trap

scenes.narration: Everyone knew that Sicily was the logical stepping stone to invade continental Europe. As Churchill famously grumbled, “Everyone but a bloody fool would know that it's Sicily.” But the Germans knew it too, and they were heavily fortifying the island.

If the Allies tried an obvious amphibious assault, thousands of young soldiers would be mown down on heavily defended beaches. British intelligence desperately needed a way to blind the enemy command and redirect their gaze somewhere else entirely.

Fortunately, the seeds of a bizarre solution had already been planted years earlier, right at the outbreak of war in September 1939. Rear Admiral John Godfrey circulated a top-secret paper within the Naval Intelligence Division that compared wartime deception to the subtle art of fly fishing.

Known officially as the Trout memo, this eccentric document contained dozens of wildly imaginative schemes to lure Axis ships and submarines into deadly minefields. But buried deep near the bottom of the list was a proposal unlike anything military planners had ever considered.

Entry number twenty-eight bore the slightly unsettling subtitle: "A Suggestion (not a very nice one)." It boldly proposed planting misleading, top-secret documents on a fresh human corpse and dropping it near enemy shores for them to find.

Although Rear Admiral Godfrey's name was on the cover, historians still debate the exact authorship, noting that it bore all the brilliant, eccentric hallmarks of his personal assistant, an imaginative young officer named Ian Fleming.

The core concept was actually an old wartime trick known as the Haversack Ruse. Armies had long used dead soldiers to carry forged maps and fake orders, fooling enemy commanders into walking straight into prepared ambushes.
Just months before, in September 1942, an actual stroke of strange luck occurred when an airplane flying from Britain to Gibraltar crashed off the southern coast of Spain.

Among the dead was a courier carrying top-secret dispatches, including a letter from American General Mark Clark to British commanders in Gibraltar. When the body washed ashore near Tarifa, Spanish authorities recovered it and quietly handed copies straight to German military intelligence.

British intelligence officers monitored the enemy's reaction through intercepted radio decrypts. They realized with absolute astonishment that the Germans had swallowed the false intelligence hook, line, and sinker.

Encouraged by this success, Royal Air Force Flight Lieutenant Charles Cholmondeley dusted off the old Trout memo concept. Seconded to MI5, Britain's domestic security service, he proposed a daring variation codenamed Operation Trojan Horse.

Cholmondeley's plan was simple yet chilling: obtain a fresh human corpse from a London hospital, fill its lungs with water, slip secret invasion documents into its pocket, and drop it from a coastal aircraft into the sea near Spain.

When the Twenty Committee initially reviewed the proposal in November 1942, they shrugged it off as unworkable. But committee chairman John Masterman saw a faint spark of potential and assigned his sharpest naval intelligence officer to take a second look.

That officer was Commander Ewen Montagu, a brilliant peacetime barrister with a theatrical flair and an unmatched eye for detail. Together, Montagu and Cholmondeley would forge an unlikely partnership that was about to change the course of world history.

London in late 1942 was a city shrouded in wartime blackout curtains, where every desk in the British intelligence offices hummed with secret plans. Amidst the paperwork, Royal Air Force flight lieutenant Charles Cholmondeley was nursing an extraordinary idea that he was determined to pitch to his superiors.

Cholmondeley had drafted a detailed proposal codenamed Trojan Horse, inspired by the ancient Greek deception. His scheme was bold and startlingly morbid: planting secret invasion documents on a corpse and dropping it into the sea where enemy spies would surely find it.

He presented his written proposal to the Twenty Committee, the secretive inter-departmental team tasked with running double agents. But the committee chairman took one look at the unusual paperwork and promptly dismissed it as utterly unworkable.

Fortunately, committee chairman John Masterman saw a faint spark of potential and assigned his sharpest naval intelligence officer to take a second look. That officer was Commander Ewen Montagu, a brilliant peacetime barrister with a theatrical flair and an unmatched eye for detail.

Together, Montagu and Cholmondeley would forge an unlikely partnership that was about to change the course of world history. One was a theatrical barrister accustomed to arguing high-stakes cases; the other was an eccentric naturalist and aviation officer with a meticulous mind.

Before they could fool the German high command, the two officers had to solve a grim practical puzzle: exactly how do you find a fresh body in wartime London? Montagu consulted the legendary Home Office pathologist Sir Bernard Spilsbury to understand the forensic realities of drowning.

Spilsbury offered reassuring advice that surprised the planners. He explained that people who died in water-related aviation accidents often succumbed to shock rather than actual drowning, meaning their lungs would not necessarily be filled with water.

The pathologist noted that Spanish examiners—being devout Roman Catholics—were naturally averse to performing invasive post-mortems unless the cause of death was profoundly suspicious. If an autopsy was conducted by someone who already assumed the cause was drowning, minor discrepancies would likely go completely unnoticed.

Armed with this crucial insight, Montagu approached Bentley Purchase, the eccentric and highly efficient coroner for the Northern District of London. Purchase warned them that while bodies were tragically plentiful, every single one had to be strictly accounted for by the legal authorities.

“I should think bodies are the only commodities not in short supply at the moment,” Purchase remarked wryly, promising to keep an eye out for a suitable candidate. But there was a catch: the deceased had to be someone with no grieving relatives who might step forward to claim the remains.

On 28 January 1943, Purchase called Montagu with urgent news. He had located a body that fit their exact requirements—a frail young man who had tragically died from accidentally ingesting rat poison containing phosphorus.

The coroner assured them that the minuscule trace of poison in the system would never be detected in a body supposedly floating in the sea for days. When Montagu fretted that the undernourished corpse looked nothing like a fit combat officer, Purchase offered a practical counter-argument.

“He does not have to look like an officer,” Purchase noted dryly, “only a staff officer”—someone accustomed to desk work rather than frontline combat. Purchase agreed to store the body safely in a mortuary refrigerator at a strictly controlled four degrees Celsius.

There was just one terrifying limitation: the biological clock was ticking. Purchase warned the intelligence officers that the body had to be utilized within three months, before natural decomposition destroyed its usefulness beyond repair.

Montagu fiercely guarded the anonymity of the deceased, later writing that although the man was a ne'er-do-well in life, the only worthwhile thing he ever did was accomplished after his death. With a corpse secured, the impossible task of manufacturing a completely fictitious human being was about to begin.

In the cold shadows of a London mortuary in January 1943, Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley awaited the most unusual recruit of the Second World War. They needed a corpse, but not just any body would do; it had to be someone whose sudden death at sea would raise no awkward questions.

With the quiet help of London coroner Bentley Purchase, they finally found their man. His name was Glyndwr Michael, a frail Welsh tramp who had tragically died from eating rat poison laced with phosphorus.

Pathologist Sir Bernard Spilsbury reassured the intelligence officers that the tiny amount of rat poison in the system would pass unnoticed during an autopsy. Spaniards, he explained, were reluctant to perform post-mortems and would easily mistake the condition of the lungs for death by drowning.

There was just one catch: the body had to be kept fresh. Bentley Purchase arranged for Glyndwr to rest in a mortuary refrigerator at a strictly controlled four degrees Celsius, buying the team a three-month window before natural decay set in.
Montagu fiercely guarded the anonymity of the deceased. He later wrote that although the man was a ne'er-do-well in life, the only worthwhile thing he ever did was accomplished after his death.

With a corpse secured, the impossible task of manufacturing a completely fictitious human being was about to begin. Every detail of his life had to be forged so convincingly that even the sharpest Nazi intelligence officers would swallow the bait whole.

They decided he would be Captain Acting Major William Martin of the Royal Marines. But why a Royal Marines officer? Because staff officers regularly carried top-secret documents in locked dispatch cases attached to their wrists by a leather strap.

To build a believable life, Major Martin needed a personal history, hobbies, and debts. Hester Leggatt and Jean Leslie set to work crafting a rich web of ordinary humanity to paper over the cold reality of death.

Jean even supplied a photograph of herself to serve as Martin's devoted fiancée, whom they named Pam. A tender snapshot tucked into a leather wallet would make the fictional major instantly sympathetic to whoever found him.

Hester poured her own emotional depth into writing a poignant love letter from Pam to Major Martin. The letter spoke of intimate moments shared in London hotels, anchoring the fake officer in a whirlwind wartime romance.

To prove the couple had spent time together in the capital, Montagu and Jean retraced Martin's supposed footsteps. They bought theater tickets, dined at fashionable restaurants, and even purchased an engagement ring from a Mayfair jeweler.

Every receipt and bill was carefully aged in trouser pockets so they looked genuinely worn by weather and use. Major Martin's wallet bulged with mundane bills, club cards, and unpaid debts that screamed authenticity.

Meanwhile, Charles Cholmondeley engineered a special steel canister designed to keep the corpse cold and buoyant during its secret submarine journey. The macabre cargo had to arrive in the Mediterranean without showing signs of artificial preservation.
As the pieces of the elaborate illusion clicked into place, Colonel Johnny Bevan reviewed the final dossier. Major William Martin was now ready to wage war from beyond the grave.

Late one stormy night, Montagu and Cholmondeley transported the sealed canister north to Scotland, where a silent Royal Navy submarine waited in the black waters. But would the German high command truly fall for a ghost?

To make a dead tramp believable as a dashing Royal Marines officer, Ewen Montagu and his team knew every detail had to be completely authentic. A man's life is made of small, ordinary habits, and German intelligence would check every single thread of Major William Martin's existence.

Enter Hester Leggatt, an experienced MI5 secretary with a sharp eye and a deeply empathetic heart. While the male officers debated grand strategies, Hester knew that a lonely officer without a sweetheart would instantly arouse suspicion from enemy counter-espionage.

To provide the face for Major Martin's fictional fiancée, the team turned to Jean Leslie, a brilliant young clerk who volunteered her own photograph. She posed in a smart uniform, transforming herself into 'Pam', the devoted woman waiting anxiously at home for her soldier.

But a photograph alone was not enough. To truly convince German intelligence, Major Martin needed intimate letters that felt utterly real, filled with the warmth, affection, and private jokes of a genuine wartime romance.

Hester poured her own memories and emotional depth into the correspondence, crafting words that would tug at the heart of anyone who read them. Historians note that these letters became the emotional anchor of the entire deception dossier.

“Dearest, I do hope that you aren't working too hard,” Hester wrote, shaping a voice for Pam that felt effortlessly genuine. Every turn of phrase was carefully chosen to reflect the quiet anxiety of lovers separated by war.

To back up the romance, Ewen Montagu and Jean Leslie took a weekend trip to London's West End to gather authentic receipts and mementos. They bought theater stubs, department store bills, and even a jeweled engagement ring.
Every item had a date and a story. A dinner bill from a fashionable restaurant proved that Major Martin had a wonderful evening in town just days before his fateful final journey.

Charles Cholmondeley meticulously placed each receipt, love letter, and identity card into the pockets of the dead man's uniform. Nothing was left to chance; even minor dry-cleaning tags were added to create a seamless paper trail.

Yet, beneath the quiet concentration, personal tensions rippled through the team. Charles found himself growing increasingly jealous as he watched Ewen and Jean share private smiles during their exhaustive rehearsals of Major Martin's history.

Meanwhile, Colonel Johnny Bevan surveyed the completed dossier with critical military precision. He knew that the Abwehr, German military intelligence, was notoriously thorough and would scrutinize every single scrap of paper.

The most dangerous element of all was tucked away inside a worn leather briefcase chained to the wrist of the corpse: highly sensitive fake correspondence between British generals discussing Allied strategy.
If the Germans captured the briefcase, they would have to believe that the Allies were planning to invade Sardinia and Greece, leaving the true target, Sicily, dangerously undefended.
With the fake life fully assembled, Major William Martin was no longer just a nameless tramp lost to poverty; he was a living, breathing British officer ready to deceive the Third Reich.
Now came the most perilous phase of the mission: transporting the body across hostile skies and stormy seas to the sun-drenched shores of Spain, where German agents waited in the shadows.

With the cold, motionless body of Glyndwr Michael safely sealed inside a specially designed watertight steel canister, the final journey could begin. Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley faced their greatest hazard yet: moving a corpse out of Britain and past enemy-infested waters.

Under the cover of darkness, the secret cargo was loaded aboard the Royal Navy submarine HMS Seraph. To keep the crew from asking awkward questions, the officers told the sailors the long metal tube contained delicate meteorological equipment.

Lieutenant Commander Bill Jewell commanded the vessel, a seasoned submariner ready for hazardous missions. He had been given strict orders by Naval Intelligence to safeguard the mysterious cargo above all else, though he had no idea a dead man lay inside.

The submarine slipped quietly out of Holy Loch in Scotland, diving beneath the surface to evade German patrols in the Atlantic. Inside the crowded torpedo compartment, the watertight canister rested securely among the heavy machinery.

Days turned into a grueling underwater test of endurance as the vessel navigated thousands of miles through heavy swells. The sailors breathed stale recycled air while the silent passenger waited patiently in his steel coffin.

Finally, after an arduous voyage skirting enemy waters, the submarine arrived off the sun-drenched southern coast of Spain. They anchored quietly in the Gulf of Cádiz, just a mile from the beaches of Huelva, where German intelligence agents operated freely.
Midnight brought the moment of execution. The crew surfaced the submarine in total darkness, cutting the engines to drift silently on the gentle ocean swell.

Lieutenant Jewell ordered the top hatch opened, letting the cool night air rush into the cramped vessel. The crew worked with disciplined precision, hauling the heavy steel canister up onto the dripping deck.
With quiet reverence, the crew unbolted the watertight seal of the canister. The cold sea air rushed inside, mingling with the preserved scent of ice and embalming fluid.
They gently slid the body of Glyndwr Michael out into the open air. Dressed meticulously in his Royal Marines uniform, Major William Martin was finally ready to step into history.

Fastened securely to the dead officer's coat pocket was the worn leather dispatch case holding the fraudulent letters. These pages contained the explosive secret that could alter the course of the entire war.
Before releasing him to the waves, Lieutenant Jewell cleared the deck and read a brief prayer for the fallen man. Even in deception, the Royal Navy afforded their unwitting soldier dignity.

With infinite care, the crew lowered the body over the side of the submarine into the dark, welcoming sea. They attached a small rubber life jacket to help keep him afloat near the surface where Spanish fishermen would easily spot him.

As the body drifted away on the gentle morning tide, Lieutenant Jewell watched it disappear into the predawn gloom. "Sail on, boys," he whispered, knowing the fate of thousands of Allied soldiers now rested on the floating corpse.
The submarine submerged immediately, slipping back into the dark depths to race home with the news. Major William Martin was now alone in the Spanish waters, waiting for the enemy to take the bait.

Dawn broke over the rocky coastline of Huelva, washing the Andalusian shore in a pale, golden light. A local fisherman squinted through the early morning haze and spotted something floating gently in the shallow surf.

The body was respectfully recovered and brought ashore, identified by the local authorities as a British officer who had tragically perished at sea. Word of the discovery raced swiftly through the diplomatic wires to the British vice-consul.

Enter Francis Haselden, Britain's man on the ground in Huelva, whose charm and local connections were about to be tested to their absolute limits. He needed to ensure the body was handled properly while keeping up an outward appearance of calm indifference.

Although Spain was officially neutral in the conflict, the coastal town of Huelva was a notorious hotbed of German espionage agents and Nazi sympathizers. Every move Haselden made was watched by watchful eyes from the shadows.

Back in London, Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley waited on tenterhooks, knowing that the entire fate of Operation Mincemeat now hung by a thread in southern Spain. Every ticking clock in the MI5 war room felt agonizingly loud.

As required by local protocol, a Spanish military doctor prepared to conduct a formal autopsy on the unfortunate officer. The medical examination would determine whether the elaborate deception could withstand intense scrutiny.

Francis Haselden worked behind the scenes with hurried diplomacy, applying gentle pressure to ensure the autopsy was managed swiftly and without overly intrusive medical testing that might uncover the truth.

Spanish pathologists, bound by traditional customs and influenced by the subtle reassurances arranged by British contacts, accepted the surface-level findings of accidental drowning following a plane crash.

Crucially, the personal effects recovered from the corpse—including the worn black leather briefcase containing the forged letters—were gathered up by the local authorities for standard administrative inventory.
But Nazi intelligence operatives stationed in Spain were already moving fast. German agents maintained extensive networks in Huelva and immediately demanded access to the recovered belongings.

Nominally neutral, members of the Spanish military and security forces were often sympathetic to the Axis cause, or simply too pressured to resist handing over sensitive intelligence documents for inspection.
In a secluded room away from official oversight, the briefcase was quietly opened and its top-secret contents were laid out before the eager eyes of Abwehr agents.
The letters between British generals detailing false invasion plans for Greece and Sardinia were carefully examined, photographed, and cataloged by the German intelligence gatherers.
Haselden watched from afar as the precious documents were covertly handled, knowing that the trap had been successfully sprung and the bait swallowed whole by the enemy.
With the documents copied and returned to the British channels as if untouched, the false intelligence began its long, urgent journey straight to the desk of Adolf Hitler in Berlin.
Deep inside German military headquarters in Berlin, top-secret signals hummed as Ultra decoders intercepted enemy transmissions. What would these radio dispatches reveal about Operation Mincemeat?

The translated text rushed to Adolf Hitler, who held absolute control over Nazi strategy. Hitler was paranoid about the Balkans, where vital oil fueled his war machine. Reading Major Martin's documents confirmed his worst fears.

Historians still debate the exact psychological tipping point, but Hitler became convinced the Allies would strike Greece and Sardinia. He viewed Sicily as a smoke screen, taking direct personal command.
Disregarding his field commanders, Hitler ordered major reinforcements northward. The German High Command scrambled to execute these orders, marching into British deception.
In London, Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley watched Ultra decodes stream into MI5. Their elaborate fabrication had completely fooled German intelligence.
Colonel Johnny Bevan watched with awe as the plan bore fruit. Every forged document was treated as gospel truth.
Jean Leslie and Hester Leggatt knew their secret contributions brought Major Martin to life, weaving a web of romance the Abwehr could not resist.
German officers cataloged every receipt and photograph from the briefcase, never questioning their arrival.
Across the Mediterranean, German infantry and armored units packed their gear, marching eastward toward Greece.
Sardinia saw an influx of defense units and paratroopers. Every soldier sent there was one fewer defending the actual target.
Sicily was left woefully understrength and starved of armor. Hitler's obsession blinded him to the dagger pointed at Italy.
Back in London, Montagu reviewed final signals with a triumphant grin. Operation Mincemeat was actively saving Allied lives.
Cholmondeley celebrated as the invasion fleet raised anchor.
Warships converged in the dark night. Soldiers slept below deck, unaware a dead tramp had cleared their path.
As the first wave of landing craft lowered their ramps onto the hostile sands, the true cost and consequence of Major Martin's fictional journey were about to be revealed in the smoke of battle.

Deceived by the false papers planted on a corpse, Adolf Hitler took the bait hook, line, and sinker. He ordered vital German divisions away from Sicily, rushing them off to Greece and Sardinia instead.
When the Allied armada finally arrived off the sun-baked shores of Sicily, they found the defenses drastically weakened. Operation Husky was underway, and the path ahead was unexpectedly clear.
The invasion succeeded far more quickly than anyone dared to hope, and with a fraction of the casualties planners had feared. The cleverest trick of the war had paid off in saved lives.
Back in London, Ewen Montagu and his brilliant team could finally breathe a sigh of relief. Their elaborate deception had worked, turning a desperate gamble into a historic triumph.
Charles Cholmondeley and Colonel Johnny Bevan celebrated the incredible victory alongside their dedicated colleagues, knowing their secret work had changed the course of history.

Jean Leslie and Hester Leggatt had poured their hearts into crafting a fictional fiancé and a watertight backstory for Major Martin. Without their vital work, the illusion would have collapsed instantly.
Yet, historians still debate the exact weight of every single factor, because wartime intelligence is a labyrinth of mirrors where truth and illusion constantly blur together.
Yet, for all the global fame of Major William Martin, the man who actually made the mission possible remained a ghost. His true identity was kept secret for decades.
Who was the frail, lonely soul whose tragic end became England's greatest deception? For over fifty years, history recorded him only as a fictitious Royal Marine.
His real name was Glyndwr Michael, a troubled Welshman who died in poverty from rat poison. He never wore a uniform in life, yet he served his country in death.
For decades, a gravestone in Huelva, Spain, bore the name Major William Martin. Visitors would lay flowers for a hero who never existed, while the real man lay forgotten.
But history has a way of righting its wrongs. Meticulous archival research finally uncovered the truth behind the man in the water.
In 1997, more than half a century after the war ended, authorities added a new inscription to the Spanish headstone to honor the quiet tramp.
Beneath the original military rank, new words were carved: “Glyndwr Michael. Served as Major William Martin, RM.”
A nameless vagrant had been given the funeral of an officer, and finally, his true identity was restored to the history books forever.

Historians still debate the exact authorship of the Trout Memo, noting that it bore all the brilliant, eccentric hallmarks of his personal assistant, an imaginative young officer named Ian Fleming.
Just months before, in September 1942, an actual stroke of strange luck occurred when an airplane flying from Britain to Gibraltar crashed off the southern coast of Spain.

Among the dead was a courier carrying top-secret dispatches, including a letter from American General Mark Clark to British commanders in Gibraltar. When the body washed ashore near Tarifa, Spanish authorities recovered it and quietly handed copies straight to German military intelligence.

Royal Air Force Flight Lieutenant Charles Cholmondeley dusted off the old Trout memo concept. Seconded to MI5, Britain's domestic security service, he proposed a daring variation codenamed Operation Trojan Horse.

When the Twenty Committee initially reviewed the proposal in November 1942, they shrugged it off as unworkable. But committee chairman John Masterman saw a faint spark of potential and assigned his sharpest naval intelligence officer to take a second look.
That officer was Commander Ewen Montagu, a brilliant peacetime barrister with a theatrical flair and an unmatched eye for detail.
Montagu consulted the legendary Home Office pathologist Sir Bernard Spilsbury to understand the forensic realities of drowning.
Spilsbury explained that people who died in water-related aviation accidents often succumbed to shock rather than actual drowning, meaning their lungs would not necessarily be filled with water.
The pathologist noted that Spanish examiners—being devout Roman Catholics—were naturally averse to performing invasive post-mortems unless the cause of death was profoundly suspicious.
Montagu approached Bentley Purchase, the eccentric and highly efficient coroner for the Northern District of London.

On 28 January 1943, Purchase called Montagu with urgent news. He had located a body that fit their exact requirements—a frail young man who had tragically died from accidentally ingesting rat poison containing phosphorus.
His name was Glyndwr Michael, a frail Welsh tramp who had tragically died from eating rat poison laced with phosphorus.
They decided he would be Captain Acting Major William Martin of the Royal Marines.
Hester Leggatt and Jean Leslie set to work crafting a rich web of ordinary humanity to paper over the cold reality of death.
Under the cover of darkness, the secret cargo was loaded aboard the Royal Navy submarine HMS Seraph.
Lieutenant Commander Bill Jewell commanded the vessel
Deep inside German military headquarters in Berlin, top-secret signals hummed as Ultra decoders intercepted enemy transmissions.
claims.note: Ultra decodes intercepted enemy (German) transmissions, not German decoders intercepting Allied transmissions.

claims.claim: The translated text rushed to Adolf Hitler, who held absolute control over Nazi strategy.
claims.note: Hitler ordered the reinforcements and held supreme command.

claims.claim: Hitler became convinced the Allies would strike Greece and Sardinia, viewing Sicily as a smoke screen.
claims.note: Hitler believed Sardinia and Greece were the primary targets and Sicily was a diversion.

claims.claim: Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley watched Ultra decodes stream into MI5.
claims.note: Ultra decrypts showed the Germans fell for the ruse.

claims.claim: The invasion succeeded far more quickly than anyone dared to hope, and with a fraction of the casualties planners had feared.
claims.note: Sicily was liberated more quickly than anticipated and losses were lower.

claims.claim: Glyndwr Michael died in poverty from rat poison and never wore a uniform in life.
claims.note: He was a tramp who died from eating rat poison containing phosphorus.

claims.claim: In 1997, authorities added a new inscription to the Spanish headstone to honor Glyndwr Michael.
claims.note: His real identity was added to the headstone in Huelva in 1997.

fact_check.summary: The script demonstrates exceptionally high historical accuracy, closely adhering to the documented facts, books, and accepted histories regarding Operation Mincemeat. The narration generally follows historical accounts of Operation Mincemeat, though it inaccurately implies that the Germans were the ones using Ultra to intercept British messages.

score.tip: Tighten repetitive summaries across sections to maintain a faster narrative momentum.
score.better_hook: Could a corpse convince Adolf Hitler to walk straight into a deadly Allied trap?
